name: Femi Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the wok station at Lantern Noodle, a busy noodle bar that's part of a little chain of six. I come in at eleven, prep my mise en place, which is just everything chopped and ready in tubs, then lunch rush is ninety minutes of fire. Afternoon I restock, then dinner till ten. I'm still slow on the toss and I scorch the garlic sometimes, so Kenji, the head cook, keeps an eye on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the speed, the flames, the sound of the wok hei, that smoky taste you only get on a proper burner. The grease on everything wears me out, and the burns on my forearms. I use AI on my phone every day, to plan my prep list, to look up techniques, even to track my savings, which are about five months now. I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a freelance graphic designer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd post that I still use it for prep lists and recipes and it's saved me maybe half an hour a day. Nothing to be scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, I was kind of excited about where it could go. But for me it's fine. Lantern's always busy, Ana's design work keeps coming, and we're putting a bit by each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, keep using the tools, and push Kenji to let me run the wok alone on Fridays. I'd keep adding to savings. I might put a small amount into an index fund, Ana's been on at me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit flat, because I like new things, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said disappointed. What were you hoping AI would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe run the boring stuff, ordering, stock counts, so cooks just cook. I imagined a kitchen where nobody works sixty hours. In AI Plateau, we're still doing stock counts at eleven at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your life now that does worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, because Ana's freelance money goes up and down month to month. And the burns, I don't want to be a forty-year-old with ruined wrists. But nothing that keeps me up.

say: AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle, and nothing to fear.
It saves me about **half an hour** a day on prep lists and recipes.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I hoped it would take the boring kitchen work.
Our money is fine, with Lantern busy and my girlfriend's **design work** coming in.
do: Keep using **AI tools** for prep lists and recipe checks.
Ask the head cook to let me run the **wok alone** on Fridays.
Put a small amount into an **index fund** each month.
feel: **Calm**, if a little **flat**, because I like new things.
S0.quote: In AI Plateau, we're still doing stock counts at eleven at night.
fieldNote: Femi is an **everyday AI user** who'd be let down by a plateau, not relieved.
His only pressures are variable **rent money** and wear on his **wrists**.
He wants technology to cut **cooks' hours**, a progressive hope tied to the tools.

steps.text: Keep cooking at the wok station and aim for solo Fridays
Keep using AI on his phone for prep lists and recipes
Start a small monthly payment into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment kitchens should get better, not cheaper. I'd post that the time saved should go to cooks, shorter weeks, not bigger profits for the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's okay for a few years, robots are slow to get into kitchens. Ana's is the one that worries me. Designing logos and menus is thinking work, and if clients use AI for that, my girlfriend's income could halve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the person at Lantern who sets up the AI ordering and stock system, so I'm useful beyond the wok. I'd help Ana move into something hands-on, maybe sign-making or printing. And I'd build savings toward six months, since one of our two incomes might wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for me, worried for us. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's look at the numbers together, no panic. We could live on my wage for a while if we're careful. Then I'd ask what Ana actually enjoys besides the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd set up the system at Lantern. Would that put other cooks at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the kitchen manager's ordering hours. I'd want the time saved to go back as shorter shifts. I'd say that to the owners, though I can't promise they'd listen.

say: Kitchens should get **better, not cheaper**, from this change.
Time saved should mean **shorter weeks** for cooks, not bigger chain profits.
think: My **wok job** is safe for a few years because robots come slowly.
My girlfriend's **design income** could halve as clients turn to AI.
do: Offer to set up the **AI ordering** and stock system at Lantern.
Help my girlfriend explore **hands-on work** like sign-making or printing.
Build savings toward **six months** in case one income wobbles.
feel: **Excited** for myself and **worried** for us, both at once.
S1.quote: Designing logos and menus is thinking work, and if clients use AI for that, my girlfriend's income could halve.
fieldNote: His own job is safe, but the **household risk** sits with his partner's **thinking work**.
He'd be the **first adopter** at work while arguing the gains go to **staff**.
He admits his helpfulness might **cut a manager's hours**.

steps.text: Set up the AI ordering and stock system at Lantern Noodle
Save toward six months of household expenses
Help his girlfriend look into sign-making or print work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income, now, not in five years. I'd be loud about it online and I'd turn up to things. I'd say it's not the tech that's the problem, it's who owns it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Ana's design work is gone by 2028, that's just true. Then I've got till 2031 before robots can toss a wok. So we'd go from two incomes to one, and then maybe to none, in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now learning to maintain kitchen machines, there's an evening course in equipment repair at the college. I'd get a job installing or fixing robots by 2030, because someone has to. We'd cut the flat to a smaller one and keep every spare penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly, for the first time in this conversation. But busy-alarmed, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Busy-alarmed. What does that look like on a Monday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monday, I'd ring the college and book the course. Tuesday, I'd sit down with Ana and the bank app and cut three subscriptions. I deal with fear by making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't fixing robots help them replace cooks like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, and I'd feel weird about it. But the robots come either way. I'd rather be the person who understands the robots than the one who's surprised.

say: We need a **basic income** now, not in five years.
The problem isn't the tech, it's **who owns it**.
think: My girlfriend's **design work** is gone by 2028, that's just true.
We'd drop from two incomes to one, and maybe **none** by 2031.
do: Book an **equipment repair** evening course at the college this year.
Get a job **fixing kitchen robots** by 2030.
Move to a **smaller flat** and cut three subscriptions.
feel: **Alarmed** for the first time, but busy rather than **frozen**.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the person who understands the robots than the one who's surprised.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as two waves hitting his **household** in turn.
He would **retrain into robot repair** despite feeling uneasy about it.
He handles fear by **making lists**, which keeps him out of panic.

steps.text: Book the college's evening course in kitchen equipment repair
Apply for jobs installing and fixing kitchen robots by 2030
Move to a smaller flat and cancel three subscriptions
Campaign for a basic income online and at meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window, five years, and we should use it for training and fair rules. I'd talk it up at staff meal, get people thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think five years is enough for me to switch on my own terms. Ana loses work around 2031, I lose the wok around 2034. I could be the robot guy at Lantern before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the repair course over two years, part-time. I'd ask the chain if I can trial whatever kitchen robot they test, maybe 2032. And I'd help Ana start a small print shop now, while there's time to build customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. There's room to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the other cooks at staff meal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the kitchen machines, don't fight them. Kenji would roll his eyes. Kenji's been cooking twenty years and hates even the ticket printer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most if Ana's work dropped first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, always rent. It's about half my wage. I'd want five months saved before 2031 so we have breathing room.

say: Five years is a **window** for training and fair rules.
I'd get workmates talking about it at **staff meal**.
think: I can switch careers **on my own terms** with five years warning.
Our two incomes fall in turn, my girlfriend's **2031**, my wok **2034**.
do: Take the **repair course** part-time over two years.
Ask the chain to let me **trial** their test kitchen robot.
Help my girlfriend start a small **print shop** now.
feel: **Anxious** and excited, because there's **room to steer**.
S3.quote: Learn the kitchen machines, don't fight them.
fieldNote: Extra time lets him plan **staggered changes** for two earners.
He contrasts himself with a **veteran cook** who resists every machine.
**Rent** at half his wage is his main pressure point.

steps.text: Do the kitchen equipment repair course part-time over two years
Volunteer to trial the chain's test kitchen robot
Help his girlfriend start a small print shop
Save five months of rent before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do this properly. Retraining, shorter weeks, public investment. I'd say I'm optimistic, and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039, I'm forty. I'd have a proper career by then, maybe running a kitchen or managing robots across the chain. Ana has time to move into something new too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking, get good on the wok, aim to be head cook by thirty-two. Learn the robot side gradually. Maybe we'd buy a small flat in a few years, while we both earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Mostly hopeful, a bit uneasy about the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a flat. Doesn't the end point make that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But a mortgage gets paid down over ten years, and we'd have somewhere to live whatever happens. I'd keep it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the end of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there's anything for people like Kenji. Twenty years in, hates machines, no plan. I'd worry about the old cooks who hate machines, not me.

say: A **decade** is time to do this properly, with retraining and **shorter weeks**.
I'd say I'm **optimistic**, and mean it.
think: By **2039** I'd have a proper career, maybe **managing robots** across the chain.
My girlfriend has **time** to move into new work as well.
do: Aim to become **head cook** by thirty-two.
Learn the **robot side** gradually alongside cooking.
Buy a **small flat** in a few years while we both earn.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, a little **uneasy** about the end point.
S4.quote: I'd worry about the old cooks who hate machines, not me.
fieldNote: With ten years, he plans **promotion** and a **home**, not escape.
His unease is mostly for **older colleagues** who won't adapt.
He'd take on a **mortgage** despite knowing the end point.

steps.text: Work toward head cook at Lantern Noodle by thirty-two
Learn how the chain's kitchen robots work, a bit each year
Buy a small flat with his girlfriend while both earn

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Ana first and me three years later, so there's no stable income to lean on. What would help is a basic income or at least proper money for training while you learn. I'd also want the chain to give cooks first shot at the robot jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the old cooks who hate machines. I'll be fine, I love this stuff. But the old cooks who taught me everything could be thrown away. Kenji's been at it twenty years and has no plan.

headlineQuote: I'll be fine, I love this stuff. But the old cooks who taught me everything could be thrown away.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old wok cook** at a busy noodle bar in a small chain, still learning his toss.
He uses **AI every day**, has about five months saved and lives with a freelance **designer**.
He leans progressive, wanting **basic income** and shorter weeks rather than chain profits.
His worry is the **household**: his partner's thinking work goes first, then his hands-on job.
He moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, planning robot **repair** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his partner's income goes first and his own three years **later**.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid training, and cooks getting **first shot** at robot jobs.
